Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Train Conductor
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Vignette:
Omar, a 29-year-old train conductor, found himself increasingly trapped by a world that felt perpetually on the brink of disaster. His life had taken a sharp turn eighteen months ago, on a cold Tuesday morning when his routine commute transformed into a scene of unspeakable horror. He had been conducting the early express into the city, the familiar rumble of the tracks a comforting rhythm, when a figure suddenly appeared on the tracks ahead. Despite his immediate, desperate efforts to hit the emergency brake, the train couldn't stop in time. The impact was sickening, a sound that would forever echo in his mind.

He had been the first responder, compelled by his duty to exit the cab and approach the scene. The air was frigid, the metal of the train and the tracks biting cold against his hands as he navigated the debris. What struck him first, and what remained etched in his memory, was the vivid, stark crimson of blood against the grey ballast, and the sight of the victim’s visible injuries. He remembered the chilling coldness of the victim's skin when he reluctantly reached out, searching for a pulse that wasn't there. That specific temperature on his skin, the sight of the blood, and the mangled form of the body became the anchors of his waking nightmares.

Since then, Omar's world had shrunk, his senses hyper-tuned to potential threats. At work, the constant need to be vigilant for track hazards or unexpected movements on the platform had intensified into an exhausting hypervigilance. He found himself perpetually superalert, his eyes darting, scanning every inch of his surroundings, convinced that disaster was always imminent. He would check and re-check his equipment, his gaze lingering on the tracks ahead, imagining every possible catastrophe. This went beyond his professional responsibility; it was a desperate, internal command to stay on guard, always.

The pervasive sense that he could not trust safety had become a heavy cloak he wore daily. His colleagues, attempting to be supportive, would offer words of reassurance, reminding him of safety protocols and the rarity of such accidents. Yet, Omar found it impossible to believe them. He would nod, feign agreement, but internally, he was certain they were wrong, that they simply didn't understand the true fragility of life. This unshakeable conviction made even simple interactions difficult, leaving him feeling profoundly isolated. He'd started declining invitations for after-work gatherings, preferring the solitude of his apartment where he could control his environment, or so he hoped.

Even sleep offered no respite. Omar found it incredibly difficult to fall asleep at night because he needed to stay alert. He would lie awake for hours, his mind racing, listening to every creak of his building, every distant siren, convinced that if he truly relaxed, something terrible would happen. He'd check the locks on his door multiple times, peer through the blinds, driven by a primal need to be watchful and on guard. The cumulative effect of this chronic sleep vigilance had left him constantly fatigued, his eyes heavy, his concentration at work wavering. He knew he was making small mistakes, missing details, and the fear of causing another accident, even a minor one, only fueled his need to stay awake and alert.

The cold touch of a metal railing, the accidental sight of a cut finger on a passenger, or even a medical drama on TV, could send a jolt of ice through him, bringing back the visceral memory of that day. He’d find himself short of breath, his heart pounding, the specific temperature on his skin, the sudden appearance of blood, or any visible injury on another person, instantly transporting him back to the tracks. These moments were frequent, unavoidable in his line of work, and each one reinforced his belief that the world was an inherently dangerous place. Omar finally sought help, not because he believed he could ever truly be safe, but because the constant exhaustion and the crushing weight of his vigilance had become too much to bear alone. He hoped, against his own deep-seated certainty, that there might be a way to live without perpetually bracing for the next catastrophe.
